**In Praise of Paying Attention**

I woke up before my alarm this morning, which is not a thing that usually happens to me. The apartment was still dark and cool, and the street outside was completely quiet except for a distant truck turning a corner. I made coffee out of habit more than desire, and then I carried the mug to the window because I did not yet know what else to do with myself. For a while I just stood there, watching the light change very slowly, feeling the warmth of the mug through my palms. Nothing important was happening, and that was precisely the point, or at least it became the point without my having to decide it. I was not checking messages, I was not planning my day, I was not rehearsing a conversation I dread having later this week. I was simply there, in a thin slice of time that did not seem to demand anything from me at all. It was uncomfortable at first, the way any unfilled moment is uncomfortable when you have trained yourself to fill them all. Then, after a minute or two, the discomfort softened into something else, something I would later try to call attention.

Across the street there is a tree. I have lived on this street for four years, and I have passed that tree perhaps a thousand times. I would have told you, if you had asked, that it is a medium-sized tree with green leaves in summer and bare branches in winter, and that is about the extent of my knowledge. This morning, because I had nothing else to do, I looked at it again, and I realized how little I had actually seen. The bark has a deep furrowed pattern on one side where rain runs down from a fork in the trunk. A small branch was broken cleanly in a storm last spring, and a knot of wood has formed around the wound. Near the base, ants are traveling in a line so purposeful it seems almost official. A pigeon landed, adjusted its wings, and stared at me with one bright eye before deciding I was not a threat. None of this is remarkable. All of it is particular. The tree had been there the whole time, living its complicated life, while I had been looking right through it, using it as background scenery for my own worries.

We are very good at looking through things now. We look through a meal to get to the photograph of the meal. We look through a conversation to get to the point where we can say what we were thinking while the other person was talking. We look through a city to get to the next appointment, through a book to get to the summary, through a sunset to get to the filter that will make the sunset look more like a sunset. This is not a moral failure so much as a habit, and habits are easy to fall into and hard to notice. Attention is the opposite habit. It is not about effort in the sense of strain, and it is not about admiration in the sense of praise. It is about staying. It is about letting a thing be itself for longer than the fraction of a second it takes to categorize it. A tree becomes not just a tree, but this tree, at this hour, in this weather, with these ants and this broken branch and this light.

The philosopher Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. I did not understand that sentence when I first read it, years ago, in a cheap paperback I bought because the cover was beautiful. Generosity, to me, meant giving money or time or help, outward actions. But Weil meant something more inward and therefore more difficult. She meant giving your full, undivided mind to someone or something else without trying to use it, fix it, improve it, or turn it into a lesson for yourself. That is a radical idea in a world that treats every experience as content to be mined. Most of us are generous in bursts, distractedly, while half our minds are elsewhere. Weil was suggesting that to truly attend to another person, without interrupting, without preparing your reply, without secretly judging, is an act of love so complete that it is almost unbearable. I have tried it, in fits and starts, and I can confirm that it is unbearable, and that, once you get past the unbearable part, it becomes something else entirely.

Children seem to be better at this than adults, not because they are wiser but because they have not yet learned to ignore so efficiently. A child will stop on a sidewalk to watch a beetle cross from one crack to another, and will crouch there for a long time, utterly serious, while adults flow around them like water around a stone. They will name the beetle, perhaps, or give it a mission, or simply watch its legs move. There is no productivity in it. There is only fascination, which is attention in its purest form. We train this out of children, gently and with good intentions, because we want them to be efficient, to arrive on time, to not get their shoes dirty, to keep moving. We teach them to keep their eyes on the goal. And then, as adults, we spend a fortune on mindfulness apps and retreats trying to teach ourselves to stand still again and watch a beetle.

Boredom is the doorway. I do not mean the boredom of being trapped in a dull meeting, although that kind can also be useful if you let it be. I mean the ordinary, unfilled boredom that arrives in the gaps between tasks: waiting for water to boil, for a train to come, for a friend to arrive at a cafe. For most of my life I treated those gaps as emergencies. If there was a second of emptiness, I reached for my phone, or I rehearsed a worry, or I replayed an old embarrassment in high definition. The phone is brilliant at this because it was designed for exactly these moments. It knows that human beings cannot stand to be alone with their thoughts for more than a few seconds, and it offers a thousand small distractions to rescue them. But boredom, if you stay with it instead of rescuing yourself, changes its character. It stops being empty and starts being spacious. The mind, left alone, begins to notice the room it is in. The light, the sound of the refrigerator humming, the feeling of your own weight in the chair. These are not exciting details, but they are true ones, and truth is a better foundation than excitement.

Walking is one of the oldest ways to practice this staying. Not walking for exercise, although that is fine, and not walking to get somewhere, although I do that most days, but walking at a pace that allows the world to show itself. When you walk slowly enough, a street you have walked a hundred times reveals itself as a hundred different streets. The bakery smells different on a rainy morning than on a dry one. The man who sweeps the steps of the library nods at a slightly different time depending on whether he has seen you before. A cat I had never noticed was sleeping in a window box, its tail curled around its paws like punctuation. I had been hurrying past all of it, with my headphones on and my jaw set, thinking about my to-do list. Slowing down does not make the world more beautiful. It makes it more real. Beauty is a bonus. Reality is the prize.

Listening is harder than looking, I think, because sound is invisible and therefore easier to disregard. We hear the refrigerator, the traffic, the neighbor's television, and we file all of it under noise. But if you actually listen, really listen, the world becomes a much richer place. Rain on a roof is not just rain; it is a thousand tiny drums playing an irregular rhythm that changes as the wind changes. A kettle beginning to boil has a voice of its own, rising from a hiss to a whistle. A friend telling a story has pauses that are as important as the words, and a tone that tells you whether she is asking for advice or simply wants you to sit with her in the sadness of it. Most of us listen for openings to speak. We listen to translate the other person's words into our own experience as quickly as possible. To listen without translating, to let the words sit in the air for a moment before you do anything with them, feels rude at first. It feels like silence. But silence, in a conversation, is not empty. It is a sign that you are actually there.

Reading slowly is another kind of attention, and perhaps the most unfashionable. We read now the way we eat fast food, quickly and mostly for fuel, skimming the surface of sentences to extract the information and move on. I do it myself, all day, because there is so much to read and so little time. But there is a different kind of reading, where you read a paragraph and then read it again, not because you did not understand it but because you want to hear how it sounds in your head. You notice a word choice. You notice a rhythm. You notice that the author has been thinking about something you have also thought about, but from a completely different angle, and that difference opens a door. A novel read slowly can last for weeks. A poem read slowly can last for a lifetime. The words do not change, but you do, and so the words change. That is the quiet magic of attention: it makes the familiar strange again, and the strange familiar, and that exchange is where learning actually lives.

Art teaches this better than almost anything else, though perhaps only if you are willing to be patient with art that does not immediately reward you. In a museum, most people walk past a painting in about eight seconds. Eight seconds, for a work that took a person maybe eight months to make, and that has survived for decades or centuries. I used to do the same, and I would leave museums feeling vaguely dissatisfied without knowing why. Then a friend challenged me to spend one hour with a single painting. It felt absurd. What could I possibly say about a painting for an hour? It turns out, a great deal, if you let yourself. You notice the way the light falls. You notice the hands. You notice the parts of the canvas the artist seems to have rushed and the parts where every brushstroke is deliberate and tender. You notice that the painting is not really about what it depicts but about how it feels to look at it for a long time. You leave that hour not an expert, but a different person than the one who walked in. The painting has not changed. Your attention has.

The same is true of faces. We look at faces all day, on screens, in the street, in mirrors, and we rarely actually see them. We see a category: tired, happy, old, young, friendly, threatening. We see the expression and we file it away. But if you look at a face for longer than is socially comfortable, something shifts. You see the small scar on the chin that you had missed. You see the way the eyes narrow when someone is trying not to cry. You see the resemblance to a parent, or to no one at all, and therefore to themselves. Photographers know this. A good portrait is not a snapshot; it is the result of a long, sustained looking that makes the subject feel seen in a way they cannot fake. It is a generous act, as Weil said. And it is available to any of us, in any cafe, on any bus, if we are willing to look long enough to get past the category and into the person. It is also, I should add, a little scary, because once you see people that clearly, you cannot unsee them, and you begin to realize how much of your life you have spent seeing shadows.

Work can be a form of attention, too, when it is work that asks for care. Cooking is a good example, because cooking punishes distraction in small but noticeable ways. If you do not attend to the onions, they burn. If you do not attend to the stock, it goes cloudy and bitter. If you do not attend to the dough, it does not rise. But the pleasure of cooking is not just in the result. It is in the chopping, the stirring, the tasting, the adjusting. For an hour, your mind is completely occupied with a single, concrete task, and therefore it is strangely free from its usual murmur. I think this is why so many people find satisfaction in gardening, in woodworking, in sewing, in fixing old bicycles. These are not efficient activities. They are attentive ones. They require you to respond to what is in front of you, as it is, rather than to what you wish were in front of you. That responsiveness is the heart of attention, whether you are looking at a painting, a person, or a pot of soup.

Nature is the great teacher, in part because nature does not care whether you pay attention or not, and therefore your attention feels like a gift rather than a performance. A forest does not need you to notice it. A bird will sing whether you hear it or not. And yet, when you do notice, when you learn the difference between the call of a crow and the call of a jay, when you learn that the moss grows on the north side of the tree for a reason, when you learn to read the clouds and predict the rain, the world becomes legible in a new way. It is not that you master it. It is that you begin to participate in it. Mary Oliver, the poet, wrote that attention is the beginning of devotion, and she meant devotion to the world as it is, not to an idea of the world. She spent her life watching ponds and hawks and grasshoppers, and she made that watching into a kind of prayer. You do not need to be a poet to do the same. You only need to go to the same place repeatedly and let it change around you, season by season, until you become part of its rhythm.

Our phones are not evil. They are tools, and tools can be used well. But they are designed, by very smart people, to capture the exact resource I am talking about. They do not want your money first; they want your attention first, because your attention can be turned into money later. Every notification is a small interruption, a little tap on the shoulder that says, look here, not there. And because the things on the phone are designed to be endlessly interesting, they win, almost every time, against the tree across the street. The tree does not refresh. The tree does not send you a message from a friend you have not seen in ten years. The tree simply stands there, being a tree, and that is not enough to compete with a slot machine in your pocket. I do not think the answer is to throw the phone away. I think the answer is to use it deliberately, and to protect periods of time when you are unreachable, not because you are important, but because you are trying to relearn how to be present. Even an hour of deliberate unreachability can feel like a holiday.

Silence is part of this, and silence is increasingly rare. We fill silence with music in stores, with television in waiting rooms, with podcasts on walks, with our own voices in arguments. We are afraid that silence means awkwardness, or emptiness, or that it will reveal something we do not want to hear. But silence is not the absence of sound. It is the presence of space in which sound can be heard. Musicians know this. They know that the rest between notes is as important as the notes themselves. Conversations know this, too. A pause after someone says something painful is not a failure to respond. It is a form of respect. And our own minds, given silence, do not become blank. They become clearer. The constant chatter of worry and planning recedes, and underneath it there is a quieter, steadier current of thought that was there all along, waiting to be heard. It is not dramatic. It is not a revelation. It is simply the mind, at rest, doing what it was made to do.

Memory is related to attention in a way I did not appreciate until recently. I used to think memory was a storage problem, that I needed a better system, a better notebook, a better app. But memory is really an attention problem. We remember what we attend to, and we forget what we merely pass through. This is why a trip taken slowly, with a journal and long walks and meals where you actually talk to the people across the table, stays with you for years, while a trip taken quickly, with a checklist and a camera, becomes a blur of photographs you never look at again. This is also why the moments we remember most vividly from childhood are often not the big events but the small ones: the smell of a particular sunscreen, the exact shade of blue in a swimming pool, the sound of a screen door slamming. A child attends completely, without reserve, and therefore remembers completely. As adults, we attend in fragments, and we wonder why our lives feel fragmentary. The remedy is not to take more photographs. It is to put the camera down and actually be where we are, for once, in full.

Love, I think, is attention that has been sustained over time until it becomes a form of knowledge. We fall in love, at first, with what we notice: the laugh, the way someone moves, the intelligence in an argument. But we stay in love, or we learn to love more deeply, because we continue to notice. We notice the small changes. We notice the bad days. We notice the way a partner's breathing changes in sleep. We notice the parts of a person that are not beautiful in any conventional sense but are true, and therefore beautiful in a deeper sense. Attention, in this context, is not a technique. It is a decision, renewed daily, to keep looking, to keep being curious about the person across from you rather than assuming you have already understood them. The moment you stop being curious, the moment you decide you know who someone is and file them away, love begins to thin. Curiosity is the opposite of filing away. Curiosity says: I do not fully know you, and I am glad of it, because it means there is still something to discover.

There is a hard edge to all of this, and I should not pretend otherwise. To pay attention is to become aware of suffering, both your own and other people's, in a way that distraction conveniently spares you. If you look long enough at a city, you see the loneliness in it as well as the beauty. If you listen long enough to a friend, you hear the grief underneath the joke. If you sit with your own thoughts long enough, you meet the fears you have been outrunning all day. Attention is not a feel-good practice. It is a truth-telling practice. It will make some things harder, not easier. But I think that is why it matters. A life lived without attention is a life lived at arm's length from reality, and reality, however painful, is the only ground on which anything real can be built. We can build a life on avoidance for a while, and many of us do, but it is a thin foundation. Attention builds on rock.

So how do you practice it, if you want to? I am not an expert, and I do not have a system. I have a few small things that help me, and I offer them in the spirit of sharing, not prescribing. I try to put my phone in another room in the morning, so that the first hour is mine and not the internet's. I try to walk somewhere each day without headphones, even if it is only to the corner store and back. I try to read one poem slowly, out loud if I can, and to let it sit with me for the rest of the day. I try, when someone is talking to me, to not prepare my answer until they have finished, and to notice the urge to interrupt as a signal to stay quiet a little longer. I try to look at the sky at least once a day, not to take a photograph of it, but to simply register that it is there, changing, indifferent and magnificent. None of these things takes much time. All of them take a certain willingness to be bored, and to let boredom turn into something richer.

I started this morning by standing at a window with a mug of coffee, watching a tree I had never really seen. I did not have a revelation. I did not hear a voice or see a pattern in the bark that explained the meaning of life. What I had was a few minutes of clear, unhurried looking, and a sense that the world was fuller than my usual glance had allowed. The tree is still there. The ants are still traveling. The pigeon has moved on. The coffee is cold. But I am different, slightly, than I was before I stood there, because I chose, for once, to stay. And staying, I am beginning to understand, is not a small thing. It is the beginning of everything else. It is how we learn, how we love, how we grieve, how we pray, how we live in a way that can be remembered, by ourselves at least, as having been fully lived.

It is the presence of space in which sound can be heard. Musicians know this. They know that the rest between notes is as important as the notes themselves. Conversations know this, too. A pause after someone says something painful is not a failure to respond. It is a form of respect. And our own minds, given silence, do not become blank. They become clearer. The constant chatter of worry and planning recedes, and underneath it there is a quieter, steadier current of thought that was there all along, waiting to be heard. It is not dramatic. It is not a revelation. It is simply the mind, at rest, doing what it was made to do.

Memory is related to attention in a way I did not appreciate until recently. I used to think memory was a storage problem, that I needed a better system, a better notebook, a better app. But memory is really an attention problem. We remember what we attend to, and we forget what we merely pass through. This is why a trip taken slowly, with a journal and long walks and meals where you actually talk to the people across the table, stays with you for years, while a trip taken quickly, with a checklist and a camera, becomes a blur of photographs you never look at again. This is also why the moments we remember most vividly from childhood are often not the big events but the small ones: the smell of a particular sunscreen, the exact shade of blue in a swimming pool, the sound of a screen door slamming. A child attends completely, without reserve, and therefore remembers completely. As adults, we attend in fragments, and we wonder why our lives feel fragmentary. The remedy is not to take more photographs. It is to put the camera down and actually be where we are, for once, in full.

Love, I think, is attention that has been sustained over time until it becomes a form of knowledge. We fall in love, at first, with what we notice: the laugh, the way someone moves, the intelligence in an argument. But we stay in love, or we learn to love more deeply, because we continue to notice. We notice the small changes. We notice the bad days. We notice the way a partner's breathing changes in sleep. We notice the parts of a person that are not beautiful in any conventional sense but are true, and therefore beautiful in a deeper sense. Attention, in this context, is not a technique. It is a decision, renewed daily, to keep looking, to keep being curious about the person across from you rather than assuming you have already understood them. The moment you stop being curious, the moment you decide you know who someone is and file them away, love begins to thin. Curiosity is the opposite of filing away. Curiosity says: I do not fully know you, and I am glad of it, because it means there is still something to discover.

There is a hard edge to all of this, and I should not pretend otherwise. To pay attention is to become aware of suffering, both your own and other people's, in a way that distraction conveniently spares you. If you look long enough at a city, you see the loneliness in it as well as the beauty. If you listen long enough to a friend, you hear the grief underneath the joke. If you sit with your own thoughts long enough, you meet the fears you have been outrunning all day. Attention is not a feel-good practice. It is a truth-telling practice. It will make some things harder, not easier. But I think that is why it matters. A life lived without attention is a life lived at arm's length from reality, and reality, however painful, is the only ground on which anything real can be built. We can build a life on avoidance for a while, and many of us do, but it is a thin foundation. Attention builds on rock.

So how do you practice it, if you want to? I am not an expert, and I do not have a system. I have a few small things that help me, and I offer them in the spirit of sharing, not prescribing. I try to put my phone in another room in the morning, so that the first hour is mine and not the internet's. I try to walk somewhere each day without headphones, even if it is only to the corner store and back. I try to read one poem slowly, out loud if I can, and to let it sit with me for the rest of the day. I try, when someone is talking to me, to not prepare my answer until they have finished, and to notice the urge to interrupt as a signal to stay quiet a little longer. I try to look at the sky at least once a day, not to take a photograph of it, but to simply register that it is there, changing, indifferent and magnificent. None of these things takes much time. All of them take a certain willingness to be bored, and to let boredom turn into something richer.

I started this morning by standing at a window with a mug of coffee, watching a tree I had never really seen. I did not have a revelation. I did not hear a voice or see a pattern in the bark that explained the meaning of life. What I had was a few minutes of clear, unhurried looking, and a sense that the world was fuller than my usual glance had allowed. The tree is still there. The ants are still traveling. The pigeon has moved on. The coffee is cold. But I am different, slightly, than I was before I stood there, because I chose, for once, to stay. And staying, I am beginning to understand, is not a small thing. It is the beginning of everything else. It is how we learn, how we love, how we grieve, how we pray, how we live in a way that can be remembered, by ourselves at least, as having been fully lived.
